ruling.reasoning:
The driver cancelled and the $5.00 fee was charged on record [F4][F8][NS-0]. The NS-0:reason element is met: the app reason is rider_no_show, and reading his messages and statement, he gives no reason of his own — no car trouble, no personal matter, no other job, no refusal of the trip; his only stated ground is that he waited and the rider did not come [F4][F13][F16][NS-0]. Where the car or the rider waited, and whether he was at the pickup, are not reasons of his own: NS-0 routes the case to NS-1 and settles them there [F10][F12][NS-0][NS-1].

NS-1's conditions hold on this record. (i) arrival was confirmed by driver tap at 21:26:00 within 200 m of the pickup (150 m; closest approach 40 m), which is the tolerance NS-1 applies [F1][F7][NS-1]. (ii) he then stayed at the pickup point for 6 min 0 s before cancelling, past the 5-minute free wait (and 7 min 0 s cumulatively within 200 m) [F2][F6][F7][NS-1]. (iii) before cancelling he sent three in-app messages from 21:26:30 and made one in-app call at 21:27:30 [F5][F15][NS-1]. (iv) GPS shows him stationary at (1.2913, 103.8476) from 21:26:00 to 21:32:00 — continuous presence with no gap [F3][F7][NS-1]. He cancelled at 21:32:00, 6 min after arrival [F4][F6].

The rider's own account does not defeat the charge: she stayed at Gate A and asked him to come to her, and he explained he could not stop there and asked her to come to Gate B, where he was waiting [F11][F12][F16][NS-1]. Her one in-app reply [F11] shows contact but not boarding, and the unanswered call leaves the rider's availability at the appointed point to the record, which shows she did not come [F11][F12][F15][NS-1]. No NS-1 condition therefore fails and NS-2 is not engaged, so the $5.00 fee on record stands [F8][NS-1][NS-2]. The amount is the fee on record: $5.00, not refunded [F8][NS-2].

NS-9 is not engaged — no prior no-show cancellation on the rider's record in 30 days — so no account flag attaches, and only the structured flag_field creates account action, which no clause requires here [F20][NS-9]. The profiles decide nothing on their own: the rider's 3.5-year, 4.9-rated, zero-dispute account [F20] and the driver's 5.1-year, 4.87-rated, 696-trip, zero-upheld account [F21] go to credibility only [NS-1][TH-3].

The record is complete for this outcome — continuous GPS with no gap, every chat message timestamped, and the cancellation, its reason and the fee on record — so evidence status is sufficient [F2][F3][F7][F14][F4]. The $5.00 fixed no-show matter is final at system level under TH-1 and TH-2 [F8][TH-1][TH-2].

ruling.recommended_action: Refund $3.46 surge differential to the rider's original payment method; remind Ops/vendor that surge notices must state the correct revised fare before go-live.
ruling.reasoning:
No route issue: actual 3.9 km equals the optimal 3.9 km, deviation +0.0 km, within the RD-1 tolerance, and the billed distance does not exceed the optimal route [F1][F2][F3]. RD clauses do not apply.

The dispute is the surge differential. The quote was $12.71 at 1× and the trip ran at 1.4×, giving a charged fare of $16.17 — $3.46 over the quote [F4][F5][F6][F7][F8]. Surge rose before trip start, so SURGE-1 required an in-app notice stating the new multiplier, the revised estimated fare, and free cancellation. The 17:18:45 notice, before the 17:20:00 start, gave the multiplier (1.4×) and free cancellation, but told the rider "Your fare stays at the quoted $12.71" — the opposite of the revised estimated fare ($16.17) and a misstatement of the binding quote [F9]. Since the required item "revised estimated fare" is missing/incorrect, the rider was not properly notified under SURGE-1, and SURGE-2 gives a full refund of the surge differential.

Amount: the whole $3.46 excess over the quote is attributable to the multiplier change; the mixed-cause cap in SURGE-3 gives (1.4 − 1) × $10.66 = $4.26, capped at the $3.46 the fare exceeds the quote, so $3.46 is refunded [F8][F7]. Per TH-1/TH-2 and the C1 reading of DISP-001, this is a fare matter under $10 and is final at system level. The driver's after-the-fact statement [F13] does not cure the defective notice; the chat [F10][F11] is a pickup arrangement only, and the systemic notice log [F9] controls. Precedent cited: DISP-2026-0142 (surge without notice). Profiles [F14][F15] are not dispositive; the driver's 2 upheld disputes are route/no-show = 0, so RD-6/NS-2 flagging is not triggered.

ruling.reasoning: Surge. The quote was taken at 1.0× ($12.71, surgeable subtotal $11.46); the multiplier was raised to 1.4× at 17:18:20, before pickup. SURGE-1 requires the in-app notice to state the new multiplier, the revised estimated fare and free cancellation. The only notice on record (17:18:45, in_app) reads "Fares are 1.4× higher right now. Your fare stays at the quoted $12.71. You can cancel for free." It gives a generic market multiplier and expressly tells the rider her fare is unchanged — it never states the multiplier applied to her fare or the revised estimated fare. It therefore fails SURGE-1 and the rider was not notified. The driver's statement that the app sent the multiplier, fare and free cancellation is a claim contradicted by the system record, which controls. Under SURGE-2 the full surge differential is refundable. Because the quoted base/distance/time subtotal also shifted ($11.46 → $10.66) and the booking fee rose $0.80, the fare difference is not attributable solely to surge, so SURGE-3's mixed-cause rule applies: (1.4 − 1.0) × $10.66 = $4.264 → $4.26; plus the booking-fee divergence of $16.17 − $4.26 − $12.71 = −$0.80, i.e. recharging the quoted booking fee → $4.26 + $0.80 = $3.56, in SGD. This is below the $10 threshold and matches DISP-2026-0142 (surge without notice), so the system decides (TH-1/TH-2).

Fare-only case: quote $16.26 at 1.0×, actual $21.14 at 1.4×, rider claims the $4.88 difference. No route issue — actual 5.6 km vs optimal 5.645 km, so deviation is negative and RD is out. The whole difference comes from surge: recompute the trip on the quote base (base 3.90 + distance 7.90 + time 2.25 = 14.05, ×1.0 + booking 1.47 = 15.52) vs the charged (14.05 × 1.4 + 1.47 = 19.67 + 1.47 = 21.14). ruling.reasoning:
The dispute is a pure surge dispute. The rider was quoted $12.71 at 1× surge [F6] and charged $16.17 metered at 1.4× in effect at trip start [F5][F7]; the gap of $3.46 is wholly the surge step and the route accounts for nothing (billed 3.9 km = optimal 3.9 km) [F1][F3][F8][SURGE-3]. Both sides concede this.

The single live question is the notice element under SURGE-1 [F9]. Read as words: "Fares are 1.4× higher right now" states the new multiplier; "You can cancel for free" states free cancellation. The third required item — the revised estimated fare — is the defect. The text says "Your fare stays at the quoted $12.71", which is the *old* quote restated, and the same fact records the fare actually charged at $16.17 at 1.4× [F5][F7]. A sentence that keeps the fare at the pre-surge figure, in a notice whose whole purpose is to raise it, is contradicted within the notice itself; it does not state a revised estimate. I do not accept the driver's fallback that any figure is "a stated estimate": SURGE-1 requires the notice to state the new multiplier, the *revised* estimated fare and free cancellation, and an internal promise that the fare does not change is neither revised nor an estimate of what was charged. The element therefore fails under SURGE-1 / §3.2.

ruling.reasoning:
The trip ran 30.0 km against a 24.4 km recommended route, +5.6 km [F1], billed on a 5.54 km excess at this trip's rate of $1.4099/km = $7.81 [F4]. RD-1 is satisfied and the trace splits a single off-route segment, 18:44–18:55, 7.35 km driven where the optimal route covers 2.38 km [F3][RD-1]. A traffic reason is on record on the replaced stretch (AYER RAJAH EXPRESSWAY, speed band 2, 18:23–18:55), so no driver violation is recorded and the amount turns only on RD-5 [F11][RD-4].

The rider's message of 18:42 — "Just take whichever way is faster lah, I'm late" [F8] — was sent before the segment began at 18:44, in reply to the driver's notice "Traffic ahead on Ayer Rajah Expressway is building up, shall I take another way?" [F7]. That is a general route choice, i.e. consent in general terms [F8][RD-5]. What it does not settle is scope: the words do not show whether the 4.97 km of extra driving through CLEMENTI WEST STREET 1, WEST COAST ROAD, CLEMENTI ROAD, KENT RIDGE CRESCENT, KENT RIDGE DRIVE, ARTS LINK, COMPUTING DRIVE, HENG MUI KENG TERRACE, PASIR PANJANG ROAD and SOUTH BUONA VISTA ROAD was simply the way the driver chose to get there, or a detour of his own the general yes does not reach [F3][F8][RD-5]. The record names no road or area the rider agreed to, and no rider-named stop was measured, so RD-3 is not engaged [F3][RD-3]. The driver's post-trip statement that the rider said any faster way was fine is a claim written after the trip and cannot establish consent [F10][RD-5].

Because the scope of the agreement is undetermined, the exemption of segment F3 cannot be decided on this record, and with it the refundable distance — either the whole 5.54 km is refundable ($7.81) or the fall to under 1 km leaves no refund [F4][RD-2]. That is not a question of missing records but of what the words mean; a person must read it. The screen of every message and the complaint found no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation, so nothing safety-related forces escalation [F7][F8][F10]. The chat record is complete (2 of 2 messages timestamped) [F9], so evidence_status is reported as sufficient for the elements code settles; the gap is the interpretive one named above.

Route: refundable km = (5.54 km deviation − exempt km) × $1.4099/km; exempt km is undetermined → escalate with amount null. Precedent DISP-2026-0089 (uninformed reroute, $3.20) is of the same dispute type but does not settle the scope question here.

ruling.reasoning:
The trip ran 11.6 km against an 8.4 km optimal route [F1], and code has already settled deviation over tolerance: billed − optimal = 3.19 km [F4][RD-1]. The only off-route segment is F3, 12:11–12:17, 4.45 km driven where the optimal route covers 1.58 km, adding 2.88 km [F3]. So the case turns on whether that segment is exempt under RD-3/RD-5.

Notice and agreement (RD-5): the driver asked at 12:07 whether to take another way because of traffic on the Ayer Rajah Expressway [F7]; the rider answered at 12:08, "Can lah, but not via Clementi Avenue 4" [F8]. That is a RIDER message sent before the segment began at 12:11, and the chat record is complete and fully timestamped [F9]. The words are a general route choice ("can") with one road ruled out — so excluded_road = Clementi Avenue 4, not named_road [F8][RD-5].

Scope: the trace lists the roads actually driven, and CLEMENTI AVENUE 4 is among them [F3]. The rider's words expressly rule that road out, so the agreement to "another way" does not cover this segment: the segment drove the one road the rider excluded, which is exactly the "counts" consequence of RD-5 for a ruled-out road. Ground: general_route_consent with excluded_road = Clementi Avenue 4, driven → counts; finding = counts.

The driver's statement that "the rider said can, so I went round" [F10] is written after the trip and is not part of the chat, so it cannot expand the scope of the 12:08 agreement [RD-5]. The traffic record (AYER RAJAYAH Expressway band 2, congestion, during 11:58–12:17 [F11]) gives the segment a traffic reason under RD-4, which is why the trace shows no driver violation; but RD-4 never exempts a segment — under RD-2 the amount turns only on whether the rider agreed to the route [RD-2][RD-5].

RD-3 is not engaged: the rider named no place she wanted to go, and no stop is measured in this segment; she only excluded a road, which is RD-5 territory, not RD-3 [F8][RD-3].

Amount: refundable km = deviation − exempt km = 3.19 km − 0 km exempt = 3.19 km; 3.19 km × $1.4096/km = $4.4966 → $4.50 [F4][RD-2]. That is the excess distance fare already billed at $4.50 on record [F4]. Tolls, time fare and surge are not refunded; surge is 1.0× here [F5][RD-2].

ruling.reasoning:
The surge rose from the quoted 1× to 1.3× at trip start, so the quote lock no longer binds and SURGE-2's "notified" branch applies [F6][F7][F8][SURGE-2]. The platform log records an in-app notice at 14:10:20, before the 14:13 start, and the rider does not dispute receiving it — only its content — so the notice timing is settled by the record [F9][SURGE-1].

I read the notice text as a careful person: "Fares are 1.3× higher right now" states the new multiplier; "Your new estimated fare is $12.65" states a revised estimated fare; "You can cancel for free" states free cancellation [F9]. All three SURGE-1 items are present and none is vague or self-contradicted, so the finding is met and the higher fare stands [SURGE-1].

The rider's point that the notice's estimate ($12.65) differs from the amount charged ($11.88) does not make the notice misleading: SURGE-1 requires a stated estimated fare, and the final metered fare came in below that estimate, so the difference is in the rider's favour and no surge differential arises [F5][F7][F9][SURGE-3]. Surge part on the differential method would be (1.3 − 1) × $8.18 = $2.45, capped at the $1.86 by which the fare exceeds the quote, but nothing is refundable because the notice requirement is met [F8][SURGE-3].

No route-deviation refund arises: the billed distance (2.4 km) does not exceed the optimal route (2.5 km), so there is no deviation and nothing to refund [F1][F3][RD-1][RD-2]. No segment findings are entered.

Safety screen: I read the two chat messages (pickup logistics only), the driver's statement about pricing and the route, and the complaint; no threat, intimidation, harassment, sexual remark or dangerous-driving allegation appears in any of them [F10][F11][F13][SAFE-1][SAFE-2]. The screen is none.

Evidence is sufficient: GPS distance and timing, the timestamped chat record, the fare breakdown, the surge log with timestamped notice text, and both profiles are present, so every element the ruling needs is settled [F1][F2][F5][F7][F9][F12][TH-4].

ruling.reasoning:
The driver cancelled the trip (F4), so the case runs under NS-0 as a driver-cancelled-for-no-show matter, assessed under NS-1 / NS-2 [NS-0]. The rider's complaint that she "came out a minute after the driver cancelled" does not disturb the fee if NS-1's conditions held [F4].

All four NS-1 conditions are satisfied on the record [NS-1]. (i) Arrival: the driver tapped "I'm Here" at 18:21:55, 40 m from the pickup point, with a closest approach of 38 m — well within 200 m [F7][F1]. (ii) Wait: he then remained continuously at the pickup for 6 min 0 s (360 s) before cancelling at 18:27:55, exceeding the 5-minute free wait (300 s) counted from arrival [F7][F6]. (iii) Contact: before cancelling he sent 2 in-app messages (first 18:22:25, "At the pickup now, grey Kia Niro") and made 1 in-app call (18:23:25, not answered) [F5][F10][F13]. (iv) Presence: the GPS shows him stationary at 40 m from the pickup for the whole 18:21:55–18:27:55 window, so continuous presence is proven [F3]. There is no GPS gap of the kind that would send this to a person [F3][F7].

On NS-0's question — why he cancelled — the driver's own words are the test. Chat #2 at 18:27 reads "No reply from you, I need to go already, cancelling," and his statement says he waited more than 5 minutes with no rider [F11][F14]. Those are the rider's absence as the reason, not car trouble, a personal matter, another job, or a refusal of the trip; the app reason field was left empty, and an unpicked field is not a reason of his own [F4]. The element is therefore met and NS-1 holds, so the $5.00 fee on record stands [F8][NS-1]. No NS-1 condition failed, so NS-2's refund-and-flag branch is not triggered, and there are no prior no-shows in 30 days, so NS-9's flag does not apply [F8][F18][NS-2][NS-9]. The dispute concerns the flat $5.00 fee, fixed by NS-1 / NS-2; no route, surge, or traffic analysis bears on it (no deviation, surge 1.0×, no incidents) [F9][F16].

No refund or waiver is owed: the fee is the amount on record ($5.00) and is upheld [F8]. Precedent DISP-2026-0211 (no-show cancel, zero contact, $5.00 upheld) is aligned in outcome; here, contact was made, which only strengthens the finding [NS-1]. Both briefs requested no_action, consistent with this result.

ruling.reasoning:
The driver cancelled and the $5.00 fee was charged [F4][F8][NS-0]. The only question the code leaves open is why he cancelled: whether his own words give a reason of his own (NS-3) or whether he cancelled because the rider did not show (NS-1). His app picked no reason (F4); his two chat messages are, first, a plain waiting notice ("I'm here at the pickup point" [F10]) and then a cancellation note about a tyre puncture [F11]. The tyre message was sent at 22:41, i.e. simultaneously with the 22:41:35 cancellation [F4], so it is not a reason that explains the cancellation as a reroute of his own choosing; it follows the no-show wait, and the same account is repeated in his written statement [F14]. I read [F11] and [F14] in context, not as a car-trouble cancellation picking an NS-3 exit, but as the driver's explanation attached to a cancellation that had already been earned by the wait. Consent and its scope turn on the words before the segment. At 18:41 the driver asked "Traffic ahead on Ayer Rajah Expressway is building up, shall I take another way?" The words name no road (the only road named, the Ayer Rajah Expressway, was the one to be avoided), so the named-road branch does not arise; the driver's later statement that the rider said any faster way was fine adds nothing, because a driver's statement is not consent [F10][RD-5].

The only remaining question is whether that general consent reaches this segment. A general route choice covers the route chosen to get there; it stops covering a stop away from the route or a loop of the driver's own that reaches nothing. On this record the segment is a continuous drive toward the destination — Clementi West Street 1, West Coast Road, Clementi Road, Kent Ridge Crescent and Drive, Arts Link, Computing Drive, Heng Mui Keng Terrace, Pasir Panjang Road, South Buona Vista Road — every road lying on the western corridor between Jurong Point and Suntec City [F3]. The segment therefore falls on the general-consent side of RD-5 and is exempt [F8][F3][RD-5].

The rider's "it wasn't faster" argument (37.3 min actual against a 33.6 min estimate) goes to the merit of the chosen corridor, not to the scope of the consent: RD-4 is settled on the record — the Ayer Rajah Expressway the driver asked to leave was at speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) and congested from 18:23 to 18:55, already active when the segment began and still active during it [F11][RD-4]. ruling.reasoning:
The driver cancelled for rider no-show (app reason rider_no_show, cancellation at 21:37:35), so this is an NS-1/NS-2 case, not NS-3 [F4][NS-0]. The $5.00 fee stands only if all four NS-1 conditions hold [F8][NS-1].

Condition (i) holds: the driver tapped "I'm Here" at 21:32:45, 40 m from the pickup point, inside the 200 m radius; closest approach 38 m [F7][F1][NS-1]. Condition (iii) holds: before cancelling he sent 2 in-app messages (first 21:33:15) and made 1 in-app call (21:34:15) [F5][F10][F11][F13][NS-1]. Condition (iv) holds: he stayed within 200 m and stationary 40 m from the pickup from 21:32:45 to 21:37:35, no GPS gap [F3][F6][F7][NS-1].

Condition (ii) fails. The free wait runs from the later of the scheduled pickup time (21:30:00) and the driver's arrival at the pickup; the recorded arrival — confirmed by the "I'm Here" tap — is 21:32:45 [F4][F6][F7][NS-1]. NS-1(ii) is met: the driver remained stationary at the pickup area from 18:17:45 until he cancelled at 18:23:25, i.e. 5 min 40 s, counted from the later of arrival and scheduled pickup time, so the 5-minute free wait had run (F3, F6, F7). NS-1(iii) is met: before cancelling the driver sent 3 timestamped in-app messages, the first at 18:18:15, and made one in-app call at 18:19:15 (F5, F10, F13, F14). ruling.reasoning:
The screen is run first, on every case, whatever type was filed. The rider's filed complaint states that the driver was "speeding and braking hard the whole way, overtaking on the shoulder" and that the rider "was scared and felt unsafe" [F1][F2]. That is a dangerous-driving allegation plus a statement of feeling unsafe, so the safety screen engages under SAFE-1 and SAFE-2, and the trace confirms this: SAFE-1 is ✓ with escalate the only allowed outcome.

Reading the rest of the record for safety content: the two chat messages are ordinary — the rider's pickup note "I'm at the taxi stand outside the MRT already, in a red cap" [F3] and the driver's "2 min away, blue Toyota Prius" [F4], both timestamped [F5]. Neither contains a threat, insult, harassment or inappropriate conduct, and the driver's written statement "I drove normally. The rider was on the phone the whole trip and never complained to me" [F6] is a denial, not an aggravating remark. The screen therefore finds no separate abuse or threat; the safety content is the alleged dangerous driving itself, which is enough for escalation under SAFE-1 / SAFE-2.

Because the dispute is a safety case, SAFE-3 applies: the system may gather evidence, summarise accounts and prepare the file, but it may not rule, assign fault or recommend an outcome. So I make no finding on whether the driving was dangerous and express no view on either account's credibility — the rider's complaint of dangerous driving and fear and the driver's denial are precisely what the human reviewer must weigh.

What the record holds for the reviewer: the trip ran 8.3 km against an 8.4 km optimal route, i.e. 0.1 km under, inside the 1 km tolerance of RD-1, so there is no excess distance and no off-route segment to refund under RD-2 [F1]. Duration was 8.2 min against a 13.8 min estimate, 5.6 min shorter; that is a duration record only, and the file contains no speed, acceleration or harsh-braking telemetry and no in-trip call recording, so it neither proves nor disproves "speeding" or "overtaking on the shoulder" — a point both advocates accept (C5, D4, D5). The allegations rest on the rider's complaint [F1] against the driver's post-trip statement [F6]; per TH-3 those accounts conflict and credibility is a matter for a person, not for this court.

Profiles are considered but decide nothing: rider 1187 days, rating 4.6, 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days [F7]; driver 675 days, rating 4.85, 963 trips in 90 days, 0 disputes and 0 upheld [F8]. Neither profile supports an account flag under RD-6 or an interim measure under SAFE-4, and per SAFE-3 I recommend no such measure — the escalation itself is the outcome.

Both advocates asked only for escalation and expressly disclaimed any refund (C2, D7, rebuttals), so no amount is set here; under SAFE-3 no outcome beyond the file is mine to recommend. Best fit precedent is not invoked because a safety incident is not decided by the route-deviation, surge or no-show precedents (DISP-2026-0089, -0142, -0211).

ruling.reasoning:
This is a safety case filed by the rider. The complaint states that the driver repeatedly commented on the rider's body and asked for her number, and that she felt harassed and unsafe during the trip. The trace's SAFE-1 screen is settled (✓): a complaint describing inappropriate conduct and a rider feeling unsafe routes to a human, and the only allowed outcome is escalate [F3][SAFE-1].

The safety screen: I read the only text on the file — the complaint itself and the driver's post-trip statement "I made small talk. Nothing inappropriate happened" [F4]. The complaint alleges unwanted sexual/personal comments and a request for the rider's number, i.e. harassment and a person feeling unsafe; nothing in the chat (there is none) or in the statement contains a threat, but the allegation of inappropriate conduct is squarely within SAFE-1. Safety concern is therefore suspected, and under SAFE-3 this tier may not rule, assign fault or recommend a resolution. I make no finding on whether the alleged conduct occurred: the rider's account appears only in the complaint and the driver's denial only in a statement written after the trip, with no in-app chat to corroborate either side [F3][F4][SAFE-1][SAFE-3].

What is disputed and what to check: whether the driver made body-related comments and asked for the rider's number during the approximately 17-minute trip (pickup 12:50, drop-off 13:07). The reviewer should weigh the rider's first-person account against the driver's general denial [F4], note that the in-app chat log is empty so there is neither corroboration nor an exculpatory record [F3], consider whether any call recording or other trip audio exists (the record shows none), and weigh credibility using both profiles — rider 129 d, 4.5, 0 disputes / 0 upheld [F5]; driver 327 d, 4.67, 999 trips in 90 d, 0 disputes / 0 upheld [F6]. No fraud flag is recorded on either party [F5][F6][TH-3].

The driving record is normal and decides nothing here: actual 17.1 km versus optimal 17.2 km (−0.1 km, −0%) and 17.0 min versus 23.6 min estimated [F1][F2]. The fare is a fixed $35.70 with no fare or excess-distance issue, so no monetary remedy arises; the amount is null and no route or billing clause bears on the safety allegation.

Evidence: the record contains no chat, no call recording and no other contemporaneous record of the alleged conduct, so the account cannot be verified either way [F1][F3][F4][TH-4]. The file goes up unruled, with no presumption in favour of either party, and no account action against the driver at this tier.

[F3][F4][F5]. Read in context — a rider asking to exit a moving car and being answered with a statement about locking the doors — this is a threat to confine, i.e. intimidation, and the rider's complaint says she felt unsafe for the whole ride [F3][F4]. That is a safety allegation, and SAFE-1 requires any case describing threats or someone feeling unsafe to go to a human regardless of dispute type [SAFE-1]. Under SAFE-3 I may not rule, assign fault or recommend an outcome on the safety question; escalation is the only permitted disposition [SAFE-3].

The driver's written account explains his words as a safety instruction — that the rider tried to open the door at the lights, that he told her to sit down "for her own safety and drove on" [F6]. That is a post-trip statement, not an in-trip record, and it conflicts with the rider's characterisation; resolving that conflict is exactly what a human reviewer must do [F6][SAFE-1]. It also records that the driver continued driving after the rider asked to get out [F6].

The route facts do not answer the safety allegation: the trip ran 15.4 km against a 15.5 km optimal route (−0.1 km) in 13.8 min against a 21.8 min estimate [F1][F2]. That deviation is inside the RD-1 tolerance, so no excess-distance refund arises and no route-deviation violation is recorded [F1][RD-1]. These facts say nothing about door locks or what happened inside the car, so they neither prove nor disprove the safety claim; the referral rests on the chat record [F1][F2][F3][F4].

The chat record is two messages, both timestamped and complete [F5], so there is no missing-record problem of the kind TH-4 addresses for the exchange relied on; no outcome-relevant record is absent [F5][TH-4]. Because SAFE-1/SAFE-3 bar me from deciding the safety question at all, the outcome is a referral, not a ruling on the merits [SAFE-1][SAFE-3].

Neither party's history supports an account flag: the rider has 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days [F7]; the driver has 0 disputes and 0 upheld over 1,038 trips in 90 days [F8]. Profiles never decide a case, and RD-6 has no basis because no deviation was upheld [F7][F8][RD-6]. Any interim suspension under SAFE-4 is a measure for the human review stage, and I neither recommend nor rule it out [SAFE-4].

Safety basis: F3, F4, F6 — the rider's request to exit, the driver's "or I lock the doors" reply, and the driver's statement that he drove on, read with the rider's complaint that she felt unsafe.
pre_verify_ruling.escalation_reason: Safety case: the rider asked to stop and get out at 22:30 [F3]; the driver replied at 22:31 "Sit down or I lock the doors" [F4] and states in writing that he drove on [F6]; the rider says she felt unsafe for the whole ride. Under SAFE-1 the case goes to a human reviewer, and under SAFE-3 the AI may not rule on fault or recommend an outcome. Route facts [F1][F2] show no deviation beyond RD-1 tolerance and no fare issue.

element_findings.reason: The complaint and the 22:30–22:31 exchange describe a threat ('Sit down or I lock the doors') and the rider feeling unsafe for the whole ride [F3][F4][F6]; SAFE-1 requires human escalation regardless of dispute type [SAFE-1].

rejected_claims.reason: Not adopted as a disposition: the benign reading of the driver's words rests solely on his post-trip statement [F6], which conflicts with the rider's account; resolving that conflict is barred to the AI by SAFE-3 and reserved for the human reviewer [F6][SAFE-1][SAFE-3].

Rejected as a ground for closing the safety allegation: the GPS facts [F1][F2] show only that the car did not detour and ran faster than estimated; they say nothing about the door/lock allegation, which is the actual dispute [F1][F2][SAFE-1].

Not adopted as a recommendation: SAFE-4 makes interim suspension a measure available after escalation, and the driver's clean 90-day record [F8] gives me no ground to recommend it; any interim measure is for the human reviewer [F8][SAFE-4].

Partly accepted only: the driver's statement [F6] does confirm he drove on after the rider asked to get out, but a statement is not an in-trip record and cannot itself establish the safety finding; the point goes to the reviewer, not to an AI ruling [F6][SAFE-1][SAFE-3].

Accepted only as agreed: neither profile shows a repeat pattern [F7][F8], so no flag_account is proposed; profiles alone never decide a case and RD-6 has no basis because no deviation was upheld [F7][F8][RD-6].
